15.0.s.en: 1. The swiftness of the prophecy's fulfillment:

15.0.0.en: “The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste and destroyed; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste and destroyed” [1].

15.0.1.en: The Moabites came from the offspring of Lot, so they are related to Israel. They dwelt east of the Dead Sea, and their land was divided into the land of Moab and the plains of Moab, which were in the Jordan valley opposite Jericho. The sons of Reuben allowed the Moabites to dwell in their cities, and learned from them the worship of the god Chemosh. There were also at times good relations between Moab and Israel: Naomi sojourned there and returned with Ruth, and when Saul opposed David, David deposited his parents with the king of Moab. Yet the Moabites bore a spirit of enmity toward Israel and Judah, and often allied themselves with the neighboring peoples against them.

15.0.2.en: The prophet Isaiah prophesies the destruction of the great cities of Moab, and this prophecy was fulfilled literally and exactly within three years of its announcement (Isa 16:14); the destruction came at the hands of the king of Assyria, suddenly and in an unexpected way.

15.0.3.en: “Ar”: a Semitic name meaning “city”; this city lay about 14 miles south of the river Arnon (Num 21:15; 22:36), and was also called Aroer (Deut 2:36). The Greeks called it Areopolis after the god of war “Ares,” and the Jews called it “Rabbath Moab”; it is Khirbet al-Rabba.

15.0.4.en: “Kir”: a Semitic name meaning “wall” or “walled city,” about eleven miles east of the southern part of the Dead Sea; its site today is the city of Karak in Jordan.

15.0.5.en: The two cities Ar and Kir were destroyed in one night, not in one day or one daytime. For when the Sun of righteousness is absent from the human soul, which is like a great walled city, the darkness of evil and ignorance comes upon it, and it loses all that it labored for through long years, and ruin befalls it. Therefore St. Paul says: “Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober. For they that sleep sleep in the night; and they that be drunken are drunken in the night” (1 Thess 5:5-6).

15.0.6.en: * Who is like that manifest one who watches and prays in secret, surrounded by a halo of hidden light amid the outer darkness? But the wicked man walks as a son of darkness; he stands in the brightness of day, and although the light clothes him from without, darkness enfolds him from within.

15.0.7.en: Beloved, let us not be deceived into thinking that we are watchful, for he who does not watch in righteousness, his watching is not counted to him!

15.0.8.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian * When man leaves (the love of) the dark world he becomes clean and pure by the work of the Spirit and by his clinging to true purity... so the soul shines forth with light and itself becomes light, according to the promise of the Lord (Mt 13:43).

15.1.s.en: 2. The shattering of the great cities:

15.1.0.en: 2 He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off. 3 In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly. 4 And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz: therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out; her soul shall tremble within her. 5 My heart shall cry out for Moab; her fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, like an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction.

15.1.1.en: The prophet Isaiah portrays what befell the great cities of Moab besides Ar and Kir, saying:

15.1.2.en: “They go up to the house (Bajith) and Dibon, to the high places, to weep” [2]. When ruin came upon Moab, many took refuge in the pagan gods, crying out with tears and wailing, hoping that they might be able to rescue them, but in vain, as the prophets and priests of Baal did in the days of the prophet Elijah.

15.1.3.en: They took refuge in “the house”; some see that Bajith means “a temple,” or “house” (bayit), that is, “the house of the god Chemosh or the temple of the god,” or bat, meaning “daughter,” that is, “the daughter of the city” or its inhabitants.

15.1.4.en: “Dibon”: a Moabite name meaning “high places” or “leanness” or “dissolution.” It is a city three miles north of the river Arnon, northwest of Aroer, called in Arabic “Dhiban”; there stood the high place of the Moabite god Chemosh.

15.1.5.en: Some translate “Bajith and Dibon” as “the house of Dibon” or “the daughter of Dibon,” as though the Moabites had fled to the temple of the god Chemosh, or his house, in Dibon, weeping and lamenting over the ruin that had come upon them.

15.1.6.en: “Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba” [2].

15.1.7.en: “Nebo” was laid waste, near the great mountain Nebo, east of the Jordan at the southern end of the Dead Sea; it is the mountain on which Moses the prophet went up to look from afar at the Promised Land, and his soul rejoiced, longing to cross over to the land of the living and enjoy the heavenly Canaan, and he died there (Deut 34). Nebo was fortified by the great mountain, a center of defense for the Moabites, but it was lost and laid waste and became a cause of wailing. In the very place where Moses rejoiced, the Moabites wailed; what rejoices the heart of the believer breaks the soul of the unbelieving denier!

15.1.8.en: They also wailed over “Medeba,” whose meaning is “waters of rest,” now called “Madaba,” about 5 miles southeast of Nebo and 14 miles east of the Sea of Lot. It was so named because it has a pool in the south, 360 feet long and wide, and there are smaller pools in the east and the north.

15.1.9.en: The prophet says: “On all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off. In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly” [2-3]. All these are signs of extreme grief (Jer 48:37; 2 Sam 3:31; Jer 4:8; 41:5; Lam 2:10). Baldness of the head points to humiliation, for conquerors used to shave the hair of captive men and women as a sign of slavery and ugliness; the cutting off of the beard is a sign of the disgrace of the priesthood and the loss of its spiritual authority and dignity; girding with sackcloth is a sign of utter despair; and weeping until the tears become like a flood means the loss of inward joy.

15.1.10.en: This is the picture of the soul that withdraws from its God to be taken captive by the evil enemy: it loses its freedom, its beauty, its authority, its dignity and its joy, and becomes like an ugly, humiliated, broken nation, finding no rest in the streets, nor on the housetops (where the pagans place their gods), nor in the squares; wherever it is, it does not feel at rest.

15.2.0.en: “And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz: therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out; her soul shall tremble within her” [4]. It is as though the Moabites fled from city to city, and their cry was heard from afar, from distant cities; the cry of the inhabitants of Heshbon and Elealeh resounds in Jahaz.

15.2.1.en: “Heshbon”: a Moabite name meaning “reckoning” or “plan.” It is the city of Sihon king of the Amorites; the Moabites took it from the tribe of Levi (Josh 21:29; 1 Chr 6:81). It is now known as “Hesban,” a ruined city on an isolated hill between the Arnon and the Jabbok, lying about seven and a half miles north of Madaba.

15.2.2.en: “Elealeh”: a Hebrew word which perhaps means “God has gone up,” about two miles north of Heshbon, now called “al-Al,” situated on a hill.

15.2.3.en: The two cities are considered to be at the far north, and were a place of dispute between Israel and Moab.

15.2.4.en: As for “Jahaz,” it is a Hebrew word meaning “a trodden place,” called “Yahsah”; it is said to be the village of Umm al-Mawalid or Khirbet Iskandar, about 10 or 12 miles south of Heshbon.

15.2.5.en: The prophet Isaiah could not bear to see what befell these great cities, and how their people turned to ceaseless crying, until Moab trembled within: “her soul shall tremble within her” [4]; therefore he says, “My heart shall cry out for Moab” [5]. He does not stand gloating over his enemies, but shares their bitterness, longing for their return from their enmity and their enjoyment of salvation. This is the mark of the men of God: sincere inward love and a deep desire for the salvation even of those who oppose them!

15.2.6.en: * If he were not wicked he would not have become your enemy. So wish him good, and his wickedness will end, and he will no longer be your enemy. He is your enemy not because of his human nature but because of his sin!

15.2.7.en: St. Augustine * Prayer for friends does not profit us as much as it profits us for enemies... For if we pray for friends we are no better than the tax collectors, but if we love our enemies and pray for them we have become like God in His love for mankind.

15.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom. The prophet says: “My heart shall cry out for Moab; her fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, like an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction” [5].

15.3.1.en: The word “fugitives” came in Hebrew in the singular form; as though the prophet Isaiah pictures for us the fugitives from the far north to Zoar in the south, the little city to which Lot fled at the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, like a single heifer three years old that has fled, as it were, from the heavy yoke to which it was not accustomed. They became like one person, with none to support or comfort him, fleeing to the small places (Zoar) and finding no refuge.

15.3.2.en: As for Luhith and Horonaim, their location is not known, but most likely they were near Zoar.

15.4.0.en: 6 For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing. 7 Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away over the brook of the willows. 8 For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beerelim. 9 For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, a lion upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.

15.4.1.en: The matter does not stop at the ruin of cities, the shameful defeat, the flight and the crying, but a famine comes upon Moab as the natural fruit of defeat in war and the destruction of natural and human resources, or perhaps as one of the signs of nature itself rising up against them. The prophet says: “For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing. Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away over the brook of the willows” [6-7].

15.4.2.en: “Nimrim”: a Semitic name meaning “clear waters”; they are springs in the valley of Nimra on the southeastern shore of the Dead Sea. The meaning here is that the throngs of refugees are so great that the oasis cannot suffice for them and their animals, so they leave their animals and take what wealth and treasures they can carry to complete the journey, hoping that they may not be in want, but they are unable to carry all that they need. Some scholars see that besides the famine that befalls their land, the enemies take possession of their wealth and treasures and carry them to their own land, leaving Moab in ruins.

15.5.0.en: All Moab is turned into a place of crying and wailing; the cry resounds in all its borders, and is heard in the south in the valley of Nimra as far as Eglaim near Kir, and Beerelim in the north. The waters of Dimon turn to blood [9] because of the great bloodshed on that notable night [Dimon or Dibon, whose meaning is blood, most likely means the waters of the river Arnon], so that no one finds anything to quench his thirst.

15.5.1.en: The remnant who escape are as though in a state of terror, facing a ravening lion that cannot be resisted [9]!

15.5.2.en: In short, Moab loses its great cities, its fields, its waters and its peace, to become a complete ruin.

16.0.0.en: 1 Send ye the lambs of the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion. 2 For it shall be, that, as a wandering bird, as scattered fledglings, the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon. 3 Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth. 4 Let the outcasts of Moab dwell with thee; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land. 5 And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness.

16.0.1.en: We have already seen the heart of the prophet Isaiah moved with deep tenderness toward Moab, so that he cried out for them. Now he offers the Moabites good counsel to set their condition right and to enjoy good relations with the sons of Judah and to taste peace and protection, by offering tribute (lambs) to King Hezekiah; as a symbol of the calling of the nations to submit to the Lord Christ, the Lion who comes out of the tribe of Judah, for there is no peace and no eternal life without receiving Him as King in our inner life.

16.0.2.en: At the end of the previous chapter it was said: “a lion upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land” (Isa 15:9), and some see that the lion may be Hezekiah, or the Lord Christ, the Lion who comes out of the tribe of Judah to reign spiritually over the nations.

16.0.3.en: The prophet himself steps forward to declare his readiness to be a mediator or intercessor with Judah on behalf of Moab, calling on the Moabites to pay tribute: “Send ye the lambs of the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion. For it shall be, that, as a wandering bird, as scattered fledglings, the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon” [1-2].

16.0.4.en: “Sela” Sala is a Hebrew name סֶלַע meaning “rock”; the Greeks called it Petra πέτρα, which has the same meaning, for it is a fortified site in the land of Edom; the Edomites used to flee to it during military sieges as an invincible natural fortress, because it stands on the summit of a mountain (Obad 2). It is now called Umm al-Bayyara.

16.0.5.en: It is as though the prophet is calling the Moabites who had taken refuge in Edom and fortified themselves in Sela to come forward with the rest of the Moabites who are in the wilderness to Judah, and to offer the lambs in Jerusalem, “the mount of the daughter of Zion.”

16.0.6.en: It is a call to every person not to think of the human arm or natural resources as a refuge. His peace lies rather in reaching Jerusalem, and offering his life as a sacrifice of love to the Son of David, the Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah. The Lion came as a Lamb to be crucified outside Jerusalem, so that we may come forward as lambs, living sacrifices, sharing His sufferings, and so enter His heavenly Jerusalem.

16.0.7.en: * “I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1)...

16.0.8.en: Perhaps it will be asked: How does the body become a sacrifice? Let the eye not look upon evil, and it becomes a sacrifice! Let your tongue not utter defilement, and it becomes a sacrifice! Let your hand not practice a forbidden deed, and it becomes a whole burnt offering...! In this way we need no knife or altar or fire; or rather we need all these, but they are not made with hands; they come to us from above. We need a fire from on high, and a knife like this; our altar is the expanse of heaven.

16.0.9.en: If, when Elijah offered a visible sacrifice, fire came down from above and consumed all the water and the wood and the stones, how much more will this happen in your case?!

16.0.10.en: St. John Chrysostom * Bring your offerings... the offerings of your own soul!

16.1.0.en: St. Jerome. Outside the Lord Christ the prophet sees the daughters of Moab crossing the river Arnon like a wandering bird that has no nest in which to settle, or like scattered fledglings that lack the shade of wings and warmth and protection [2]; but by receiving Him we come under the wings of His Cross, and find our rest and peace and inward satisfaction.

16.2.0.en: The prophet also offers counsel to the elders of Judah, calling on them to receive the Moabite refugees who take refuge with them and give them shade in the midst of the noonday, so that the time becomes for them like a night of rest from the sun of trials and afflictions; and to hide the outcasts and the fugitives who flee to them without deceit, and not to deliver slaves to the enemies [3-4].

16.3.0.en: It is fitting for the men of Judah to bear a symbol of the Lord Christ, the true refuge, and open their hearts and their cities to the fugitives, and receive them sincerely; thus they proclaim the kingdom of Christ, established upon the throne of mercy forever: “And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness” [5].

16.3.1.en: Thus the prophet offers us a Messianic text, declaring that the Church, the tabernacle of David, is the place of deliverance, in which the Messiah reigns to draw the nations to Himself, so that they may find truth in Him and enjoy the divine mercies, singing: “Justice and truth are the foundation of thy throne; mercy and truth go before thy face... for the LORD is our shield, and the Holy One of Israel is our king” (Ps 89:14, 18).

16.4.0.en: 6 We have heard of the pride of Moab, who is very proud: his greatness, his pride, his arrogance, the vanity of his boasting.

16.4.1.en: The prophet Isaiah offered good counsel to Moab, as the prophet Daniel also offered his counsel to Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 4:27)... and at the same time he disclosed their spiritual weakness, that is, pride, as an obstacle to their accepting counsel. “We have heard of the pride of Moab, who is very proud: his greatness, his pride, his arrogance, the vanity of his boasting” [6]. The prophet had heard of the pride of the Moabites, their excessive haughtiness and their empty (vain) words!

16.4.2.en: Pride destroys man as it does nations; it deprives its owner of accepting good counsel, and makes him lose the enjoyment of God's grace and mercy.

16.5.0.en: 7 Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl: for the foundations of Kirhareseth shall ye mourn; surely they are stricken. 8 For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah: the lords of the heathen have broken down the principal plants thereof, they are come even unto Jazer, they wandered through the wilderness: her branches are stretched out, they are gone over the sea. 9 Therefore I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer the vine of Sibmah: I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh: for the shouting for thy summer fruits and for thy harvest is fallen. 10 And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting: the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease. 11 Wherefore my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kirharesh. 12 And it shall come to pass, when it is seen that Moab is weary on the high place, that he shall come to his sanctuary to pray; but he shall not prevail. 13 This is the word that the LORD hath spoken concerning Moab since that time. 14 But now the LORD hath spoken, saying, “Within three years, as the years of an hireling, the glory of Moab shall be contemned, with all that great multitude; and the remnant shall be few and small, not great.”

16.5.1.en: The leaders of Moab did not listen to the voice of the prophet Isaiah because of their pride and their conceit in their own opinion, so they fell under bitter punishments and deserved the woes in which the following is to be noticed:

16.5.2.en: a. A universal wailing: “Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl” [7]; for wailing became a general mark throughout all Moab.

16.5.3.en: b. The wailing included the greatest cities such as Kirhareseth [7], which was stricken, and also the fields that withered, such as the fields of Heshbon and the vine of Sibmah and Jazer [8-9]; it included cities and villages, the learned and the ignorant, rich and poor, and so on...

16.5.4.en: Heshbon, Sibmah and Jazer were famous for the richness of their vineyards.

16.6.0.en: c. The joys of the harvest were turned into weeping and mourning; instead of the joyful shouts of the feast, the bitter cries of battle were heard [10].

16.7.0.en: d. The Moabites went to the high place to pray in the temple of the god Chemosh, to no avail [12].

16.8.0.en: e. The time of the punishment was fixed at three years, during which Moab collapses before Sennacherib king of Assyria, and the Moabites are humiliated and their glory shattered [14].

16.8.1.en: This is the end of the proud man: he becomes like Moab, wailing comes upon his life as a whole, in great matters and small alike; he knows no inward joy nor gladness of heart, his feasts turn into sorrows, his worship is without profit, and he collapses day by day until he loses his glory entirely.

16.8.2.en: Amid this gloomy picture the prophet Isaiah discloses two cheering aspects. The first is the prophet's sharing the troubles of the sons of Moab, for he says: “Wherefore my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kirharesh” [11]. His inmost being cannot bear to see suffering souls, even if their sufferings are the fruit of their sins.

16.8.3.en: The second aspect is the existence of a remnant, very small and exceedingly feeble [14]: in ancient times Ruth the Moabitess enjoyed salvation, as she came to take refuge under the shadow of God, and in the New Testament the Gentiles came to faith to enjoy the new life in Christ Jesus.
